name: Pasaia
title: Pasaia Ship Thickness Gauging | UTM in a Narrow Basque Bay
description: Thickness gauging in Pasaia for steel carriers, coasters, fishing and offshore support vessels: hull plating, tanks and pre-docking UTM readings.
h1: Ultrasonic Gauging for Ships and Fishing Vessels at Pasaia
intro: Pasaia is a small, steep-sided harbour on the Basque coast near San Sebastián, reached through a narrow channel and shared by a fishing fleet, coasters, steel and vehicle carriers and local shipyards. Space is tight and berths are limited, so planning matters. Our gauging technicians travel from India to the ship, and each job is organised around the tide, the berth and the vessel's call length.

highlights.h: A harbour with a narrow gate
highlights.p: Ships enter Pasaia through a tight channel between steep headlands, and berthing windows depend on tide and weather. We build the gauging plan around the confirmed berth time, not an assumed one.

The mix here includes fishing vessels, offshore and wind support craft, and general cargo coasters. Smaller hulls, higher stress per plate and hard working lives make hull readings valuable ahead of repairs.

Steel products and vehicles keep conventional cargo ships and carriers calling. We gauge holds, decks and ramps while cargo operations leave spaces clear, and report in the format the owner or surveyor needs.

port.h: Pasaia: a deep bay behind a narrow entrance
p: Pasaia, also written Pasajes, is a natural harbour at the mouth of the Oiartzun river on the eastern end of the Basque coast. The entrance is a narrow channel between steep hills, so approach and departure are controlled, pilotage is used and larger vessels move only when the tide, the swell and the wind allow it. Inside, the bay opens into quays on either side, with the old fishing communities of San Pedro and Pasai Donibane facing each other across the water. Space for manoeuvring is limited, which keeps ship size modest by comparison with Bilbao.

The port's traffic is varied but not large. A fishing fleet still operates from the harbour, steel products are shipped and received for the Basque and Navarre industries, and vehicles and general cargo pass through for local manufacturers. Coasters and short-sea ships make up much of the cargo traffic, and the harbour also serves offshore support craft, wind-farm service vessels, pilot boats and tugs. The Autoridad Portuaria de Pasaia has been developing an outer harbour on the open coast beside the bay to take larger ships in future.

Inspection work is therefore weighted towards smaller hulls with demanding duty. Fishing vessels and workboats spend long periods at sea in heavy weather, then lie alongside for short repair stops. Coasters and steel carriers have holds that take hard use, and older ships on regional trades show corrosion in ballast tanks and cargo spaces. Owners of those ships want clear readings before they commit to a yard period, and the compact harbour makes it straightforward to gauge alongside once a berth is agreed, as long as the schedule leaves slack for the tide.

facilities.h: Where gauging is realistic in and around Pasaia
p: The practical locations are the cargo quays and lay-by berths inside the bay. Steel and general cargo ships at the commercial quays are gauged once holds are clear, with deck, coaming and hold frame readings taken between discharge and loading. Vessels from the fishing and offshore sectors are gauged at the repair quays and fish-dock berths when crews are ashore and tanks can be emptied. Vehicle carriers use their own quay, where ramp and deck structure can be measured while no vehicles are on board.

Drydock facilities in Pasaia are modest and suited to small craft, and several yards along the Basque coast, including those in the Bilbao area, handle larger vessels. An owner commonly gauges in Pasaia, sends the steel list to the chosen yard and has technicians attend the dock for post-blast readings. Anchorage work in the bay is limited by space, and the open roads outside are exposed in winter, so alongside gauging is the normal arrangement and is planned around the pilot's schedule for entering and leaving.
list: Commercial cargo quays: hold frame, coaming and deck gauging on steel carriers and general cargo ships between cargo operations
Vehicle and ro-ro quay: ramp, deck plating and side shell readings on car carriers
Fishing harbour berths: hull, tank and deck plating readings on fishing vessels during short stops ashore
Repair quays and slipways: workboats, tugs, wind-farm and offshore support vessels hauled or lying for repair
Lay-by berths inside the bay: coasters waiting for cargo, a survey or a yard slot
Basque and Cantabrian yards: docking-stage gauging after the steel list is prepared from Pasaia readings

context.h: Basque coast regulation and the small-ship picture
p: Ships calling at Pasaia are inspected under the Paris MoU system, with Spanish inspectors drawn from the Capitanía Marítima operating under the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Coasters and general cargo ships on regional trades have a high profile in port state control statistics across Europe, and inspectors look closely at structure, load line items and the condition of steel that holds the ship together. Fishing vessels fall under separate regimes, but owners increasingly commission thickness readings for insurance, sale and repair planning in the same way as merchant owners.

EU rules reach small ships as well. The Ship Recycling Regulation's Inventory of Hazardous Materials applies to vessels calling at EU ports, which prompts some owners of older coasters to review structure and materials together before a sale or a decision to scrap. Offshore wind and energy activity around the Bay of Biscay has also increased demand for service craft, and owners converting or chartering such vessels often ask for hull condition evidence first. Gauging provides measured thickness at the plates that matter, rather than an assumption drawn from age.

jobs.h: The kind of gauging work seen at Pasaia
jobs.p: Jobs here are usually smaller in scope than at big ports, and decided at short notice around a repair stop or a sale. A typical request names the vessel, the berth and a window of a few days, and the work is sized to fit. Technicians bring gauges and magnetic particle equipment from India, and a small team is normally enough. Examples of requests include:
list: Hull plating and ballast tank readings on a steel carrier before a yard period, producing a steel estimate for the repairing yard.
Hull and deck gauging on a fishing vessel lying at the fish dock, with attention to the shell near the waterline and the fish hold boundaries.
Hold frame and coaming gauging on a general cargo coaster between a steel discharge and the next loading.
Ramp, deck plating and side shell readings on a car carrier at the vehicle quay, with magnetic particle testing at hinge connections.
Condition gauging of a wind-farm service vessel being considered for charter, covering hull, tanks and main deck.

logistics: Technicians usually fly from India to Bilbao through a European hub and continue by road along the coast, while San Sebastián's small airport and Biarritz across the French border are alternatives depending on connections. The ship's agent arranges pilotage and quay access. Visits to Spain need a Schengen visa, so the team plans around visa issue and the call dates, and keeps a margin because tide and swell can move the berthing time of ships entering through the narrow channel.

faqs.q: Is Pasaia suited to gauging larger merchant ships?
faqs.a: The harbour is built for small and medium ships, so most gauging is on coasters, steel carriers, car carriers, fishing vessels and offshore craft. Larger vessels on the Basque coast generally call at Bilbao. We will tell you if a ship's size or draught makes Pasaia the wrong place for the planned programme.

faqs.q: Can a fishing vessel be gauged while it is ashore for a short stop?
faqs.a: Yes, if the tanks and fish holds can be emptied and ventilated and the crew has made the spaces safe. We measure the shell, the deck plating and the hold boundaries, and report where thinning is concentrated. Short stops need a tight plan, so we agree priorities with the owner or skipper beforehand.

faqs.q: Does the narrow entrance cause delays for gauging plans?
faqs.a: It can. Ships move in and out under pilotage and within tide and swell limits, so berthing times sometimes shift. We schedule technicians with some flexibility and update the plan with the agent, because arriving a day early is easier to manage than chasing a ship that has already sailed.

faqs.q: Where do ships from Pasaia go for a drydocking?
faqs.a: Small craft can be handled locally, but larger ships usually go to yards in the Bilbao area or elsewhere on the Cantabrian coast. Gauging in Pasaia before the move gives the yard a steel list in advance, and technicians can follow the ship to the yard for post-blast readings if the owner wants them.

faqs.q: Can steel carriers be gauged between discharge and loading?
faqs.a: Often, if the gap is long enough for holds to be cleared and entered safely. We prioritise frames, coamings and the tank top areas that matter most for the next survey, and we tell the chief officer how long each hold needs. A short gap means a shorter programme rather than a rushed one.
